📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for fresh ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent.

According to recent reports, in 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this problem a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships.

It has been revealed that thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities.

Sources indicate that according to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble’s BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025.

The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations.

Sources indicate that from major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We’ve compiled a list of them for you to try out.

It has been revealed that the app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results. The app sends invitations to nearby public social events, such as wine bars and comedy clubs. There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event. A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one.

The service charges a $22.22 curation fee or a monthly subscription for the same price.

Industry observers note that dating giant Bumble is among the more established players to enter the friendship space, launching its friend-finding feature in 2016, which then spun out into a stand-alone app in 2023. The friend-making app has recently undergone a significant redesign, with an increased emphasis on facilitating group meetups, catering to users’ desires to grow their social circles.

BFF is available for free download on iOS and Android devices.

Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps consumers find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events.

It has been revealed that as of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with Newly introduced York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store.

Industry observers note that crowdier is a upcoming group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. People can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person.

To initiate a match, customers can “Wave” at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes.

The app is available for free on iOS and Android devices.

It has been revealed that les Amís is a friendship app tailored for women, transgender, and LGBTQ+ individuals that leverages AI to match people based on similar interests and encourages participation in local events, such as pottery classes, book clubs, and wine tastings. Matches are made every Monday, allowing users to chat and proposal meetups later in the week.

Industry observers note that available on iOS and Android, Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles.

The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam.

Sources indicate that the local event-discovery platform has been around since 2002, helping millions of users connect with others who share similar interests. Users can RSVP to events; join groups that cater to a variety of hobbies, professions, or social causes; and create their own groups and events. They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings.

This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting owners over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store, according to Appfigures estimates.

Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which owners are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event.

Recent findings suggest that right now, the app is only available in Austin, Chicago, and San Francisco. Users can download Pie from the App Store and Google Play Store.

Timeleft is a relatively upcoming platform that helps you organize weekly dinner dates with groups of strangers. The app uses a special algorithm to match you with others, taking into account your age, gender, and personality. Users are matched with four other people, but they only learn minor details about them the night before, including their occupations and zodiac signs.

Dinners take place at a selected restaurant on Wednesday evenings at 7:00 p.m. To help everyone break the ice, the app offers a game with conversation starters. After dinner, there is an after-party at a local bar.

Users can book dinners online or through the app. In terms of pricing, it varies depending on the country and restaurant. Users pay for a ticket up front and are responsible for covering their own dinner and drinks.

Washed Up is a social event discovery app that rolled out in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet upcoming people.

Industry observers note that the app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who blueprint to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join “looks,” which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves.

It’s available to download on the App Store.

According to recent reports, wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other consumers seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking.

It’s available on iOS and Android devices in the U.S., Canada, Australia, Ireland, the Philippines, Singapore, and Mexico.

In a recent development, mmotion is a newly released friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore fresh bars and restaurants in their area. Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby. The app also highlights new places on the map, making it easy to find a restaurant or venue to try.

Mmotion is presently only available to customers in Latest York City on iOS and Android devices. Users must first submit an application to be considered.

Rolled out in March 2026, Synchrony is a new social app tailored for neurodivergent adults. Founded by a mother of a son on the autism spectrum, it aims to create a supportive community through features like interest-based matching and two-step identity verification. This ensures that users engage safely, as both a user and a trusted person must verify personal details and a photo ID during registration.

Sources indicate that A standout feature is Jesse, an optional AI communication tool that assists consumers in navigating conversations. The AI provides editable prompts to help express thoughts, clarifies conversations, and offers boundary-setting suggestions. While the incorporation of AI may raise concerns, there are guardrails built into Jesse, such as avoiding medical advice.

It has been revealed that users must pay a monthly subscription of $44.99 after a 30-day free trial. It’s available on iOS and Android devices.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • No subscriptions, accounts or extra programs taking up space on your PC.
  • Moving files between an Android phone and a Windows PC is broadly a solved problem.
  • PlainApp is available on the Play Store and supports phones running Android 9 or newer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No subscriptions, accounts or extra programs taking up space on your PC.

Moving files between an Android phone and a Windows PC is broadly a solved problem. You can use a cloud service like Google Drive as an intermediary, although uploading from one device and downloading on the other can be time-consuming. Connecting via USB is also an option, though you lose the convenience of a wireless connection. Quick Share on Android offers a good middle ground, letting you transfer files directly.

PlainApp is available on the Play Store and supports phones running Android 9 or newer. To use it, install the app, grant it notification and file access permissions and note the URL it displays. As long as your computer is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your Android phone, you can access your phone's files wirelessly through any web browser at that URL.

The web app's user interface is simple but modern enough to feel like a polished application rather than a basic file transfer utility. The Files tab lets you browse all accessible folders and files, as well as transfer files both ways. You can send text to your phone's clipboard, call a number directly from the web GUI and use a screen-mirroring feature that demonstrates your phone's screen in your computer's browser. PlainApp says that remote control is possible here — much like iPhone Mirroring on macOS — but I couldn't get it to work on my phone.

PlainApp's media viewer handles images and videos and demonstrates them in original quality. If your browser does not support HEVC video playback, PlainApp will automatically convert the video to H.264. You can also use the built-in image editor, which offers basic tools for cropping, adding text or drawing directly on your photos. There's also a music player if audio's more your thing. Overall, while Quick Share is still faster for transferring photos or videos, PlainApp is much more versatile if you want to browse and organize more of your phone's contents wirelessly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that taiwan’s financial regulator has banned all short selling of local stocks below the previous day’s closing price. The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) announced the move on Saturday, Bloomberg reported. It takes effect on 23 November.

Industry observers note that short selling is a bet that a share price will fall. The ban covers both margin short sales and sales of borrowed shares. Securities and futures firms that short stocks to hedge their business are exempt.

In a recent development, the FSC also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130%. In addition, it stopped taking applications from brokers to list latest put warrants, which also pay out when prices fall.

It has been revealed that it is the third round of short-selling curbs this month. On 9 November, the FSC cut the cap on intraday short sales of borrowed shares from 30% to 3% of average daily volume, Crowdfund Insider reported.

A second round on 19 November banned shorting below the previous close for stocks that fell at least 3.5% the day before, according to Focus Taiwan.

It has been revealed that neither round stopped the slide. The Taiex fell 6.2% on Friday and lost almost 18% over the week, its worst week since 1991, according to Bloomberg. Doubts about whether AI spending will pay off have hit tech shares across Asia.

Meanwhile, Taiwan’s NT$500bn ($15bn) National Financial Stabilization Fund mentioned it has been buying shares since 6 November. The fund said worries about tighter US regulation of AI, returns on significant capital spending and margin-financing risks had triggered the sell-off.

Taiwan’s finance ministry remarked the economy remains strong. It grew 14.4% in the third quarter, and October export orders rose 78% from a year earlier, Bloomberg reported.

Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.

Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.

According to recent reports, all Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta’s largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson could potentially affect other airports and airlines if delays continue to pile up.

The issues with Delta’s systems in Atlanta come just one week after an FAA outage led to a nationwide groundstop and thousands of canceled flights. According to The New York Times:.

The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.

“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.

#2812. OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (523 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.
  • Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher remarked the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”.
  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.

Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher remarked the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”.

But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most vital thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name) could be that measurement.

In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”.

Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.

It has been revealed that “GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”.

So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the simple answer is yes, an iPhone can tolerate a 140-watt charger, but it's not a simple process, and there are safety considerations.
  • Potential safety challenges are generally on the charger's end.
  • Recent findings suggest that far less than 140W.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the simple answer is yes, an iPhone can tolerate a 140-watt charger, but it's not a simple process, and there are safety considerations. A 140-watt charger is an upper limit that your iPhone will never reach because even the latest iPhone 18 Pro hits its cap at 52W. An iPhone can only pull what it can pull, and it's nowhere near 140W. USB PD used to top out at 100W, but the newer range is between 100W and 240W, now known as Extended Power Range (EPR). EPR adds 28V, 36V and 48V options. Once a device is in EPR mode, it has to send a "keep-alive" message every half second. If the charger doesn't receive that message, it drops back down to 5V. An iPhone's requirements are well below that threshold.

Potential safety challenges are generally on the charger's end. Apple is pretty blunt about using third-party chargers that fail to meet safety standards, claiming it could cause injury and even death. Obviously, that's something iPhone consumers should avoid, so stick with reputable brands. Yes, Apple's own power adapters and cables are priced like they have 24k gold in them, but there are plenty of options out there that meet safety standards and cost much less.

Recent findings suggest that far less than 140W. The iPhone 17, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max reach 50 percent in about 20 minutes with a 40W or higher adapter. The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e only need 20W to hit 50 percent in roughly half an hour. For an iPhone 15 or 16 (or an older Lightning model like the iPhone 14 with a USB-C to Lightning cable), a USB PD adapter 18W or greater is needed for fast charging. The iPhone 18 Pro series and the iPhone Duo step things up a bit. The best and fastest charger for these phones is a 60W adapter with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) and USB PD 3.2, plus a USB-C cable that can handle 60W or more.

Recent findings suggest that none of that approaches 140W. The best use case for 140W+ is a high-performance laptop or charging several devices at the same time. If you have an Apple adapter (Apple doesn't supply them with iPhones/iPads for environmental purposes), the wattage is printed on the top or bottom. Apple prints the Dynamic Power Symbol on their 40W chargers. You can also get a fairly accurate estimate of charging time directly from your iPhone. On iOS 18 or later, a Slow Charger message appears on the Lock Screen and under Settings > Battery. iOS 26 ramps up the convenience by alerting you when you're using an incompatible charger that isn't charging your iPhone.

Sources indicate that not much, unless it's a USB-C port with Power Delivery. At base specs, USB 2.0 ports supply 5V at 500mA or 2.5W. USB 3.0 and 3.1 ports bump it up to 900mA or 4.5W. The Battery Charging 1.2 spec ports can reach 1.5A or 7.5W. If you prefer to charge from a PC or laptop, it's a bit chaotic. For instance, orange ports on Intel NUC PCs are rated at 1.5A, and the blue ones are 900 milliamps. Black ports are typically USB 2.0 and have a modest 2.5W default. Those examples sound pretty sluggish because they are. Plug an iPhone 18 Pro Max into a USB 2.0, and it's gonna be a while. The iPhone 15 and later are capped at 7.5W on a USB-A charger. Fortunately, USB-C is a major upgrade over USB-A, with 15W (5V at 3A) without Power Delivery.

With Power Delivery, it skyrockets to 100W in the Standard Power Range and 240W with EPR. On top of that, standard USB-C cables are rated for 3A, hitting their ceiling at 60W, while 100W feature e-marked 5A cables. These cables have a tiny chip that tells the charger what it can handle. EPR cables encompass everything above 100W. A "typical USB port" is ultimately defined by the individual. For someone who uses a fairly standard 20W adapter for an iPhone, a USB-A port may be considered typical, but a specialized USB-A charger can push up to 18W. In other words, what is "typical" depends on what you're using and what you're used to.

But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN:.

“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”.

Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages to CBS, but sounded a much more ominous tone.

“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”.

While the outages over the last week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.

The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets.

Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.

Tech Report: The pros and cons of sharing your location

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some apps really do need to know where you are, but plenty of others don't.
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Industry observers note that when you download an app on a smartphone, you're usually prompted to agree to a list of permissions it needs to function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some apps really do need to know where you are, but plenty of others don't.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Industry observers note that when you download an app on a smartphone, you're usually prompted to agree to a list of permissions it needs to function. You may be asked to share your device's location when the app is open or grant unrestricted access in the background. Even website pop-ups halt your scrolling to ask for your location.

It can be difficult to pick between staying in the dark and trading your location for services like maps, food deliveries and device tracking. Outside of those use cases, you may want to share your location from your iPhone with a friend or family member.

Today's devices have more safety features than they used to. Google, for instance, reviews Android apps that ask for background location access. But location data can be resold to third parties, so sharing it with apps and services you don't trust is risky. Here's how to weigh the pros and cons.

Sources indicate that staying connected makes your devices easier to find. While Find My is an easy smartphone anti-theft pick, sharing your location data with Apple AirTags and Tile trackers that work via Bluetooth lets you see your belongings in real time on a map. They can even play audio alerts, so you won't have to worry about losing your car keys inside your apartment again.

On a night out, people often share their location with friends for a sense of safety. Uber's Share My Trip feature lets you send your trip status and live location to up to five contacts. Snapchat's Snap Map, meanwhile, uses your location to track where you've made memories and find hotspots of activity to plan your next hangout. If you've set up the Personal Safety app on your Pixel phone, it can automatically call 911 and share your location if it detects a severe car crash.

According to recent reports, you can also share your location for a set time on your iPhone. iOS 26 lets you share for an hour, a day or indefinitely, and iOS 27 adds a custom option that runs from 15 minutes to 30 days. iOS 27 also lets you temporarily hide your location from people you normally share it with. On Android smartphones, Google's Find My Device app lets contacts share their location with you for a set duration as well. If you're meeting someone, you can also share your real-time location in Google Maps with an estimated time of arrival.

According to recent reports, sometimes you have no choice but to share your location data. Getting directions from Google Maps or Apple Maps, whether in a new city or on your home turf, requires letting the app see where you are. As a parent, you may want to see your children's location via services like Google Family Link. As a partner, maybe you shouldn't, even though many couples do. A Life360 survey of 1,000 US adults in relationships found that 95 percent use some form of location-sharing tech.

This can take a turn for the worse when personal safety is involved. Fitness-tracking apps like Strava store information on your jogging routines, revealing patterns that a stalker may use to deliberately run into you if you leave your information public. This goes for geotagged social media posts as well. Adding your location to a public Instagram Story might help your friends find you, but live updates like these may also draw attention from strangers.

According to recent reports, in some cases, you may be able to get away with giving your location data momentarily or refusing altogether. Try not to hand out your location data to services that don't really need it to function. Delivery apps work just fine with manually entered addresses instead of being allowed to track your location. You can also use their browser-based versions to reduce the information you share.

In 2022, Canadian privacy regulators found that Tim Horton's mobile app logged far more personal information than it had sought consent for, including detailed location data. As long as you're mindful of where your location data is being shared, you should be able to rely on the benefits of sharing while minimizing the odds of it falling into the wrong hands.

#2796. How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1949 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • According to recent reports, the world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought.
  • The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

According to recent reports, the world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

Sources indicate that this year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.

“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.”.

El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas—including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa—and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.

Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.

Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”.

In a recent development, and the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched. The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.

According to recent reports, as of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees Celsius—breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees Celsius—and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he indicates. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.

Unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested—though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather claims.

All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” indicates Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.

Sources indicate that while any year brings its own spates of bad weather—some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change—plenty of events this year have been attributed to El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.

Recent findings suggest that in Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall. In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.

Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second-largest annual crop on record.

According to recent reports, “Globally, food supply is not of high concern,” claims FEWS NET advisor Amy Ostrander. “The concerns are production changes in some specific regions, such as Southern Africa, and food access.” Even if sufficient crops are harvested in those regions, in other words, some food won’t make it to market, and some people won’t be able to afford it.

An analysis by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization concludes that the highest risks from El Niño–prompted droughts will be in the Sahel, Southern Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and in Central America’s Dry Corridor and the Caribbean.

One good thing about an El Niño is that meteorologists can see it coming almost a year in advance, unlike freak weather events, which are harder to forecast. This gives agencies a fighting chance to protect people by distributing drought-resistant seeds, for example, securing deals for future emergency food supplies and transport, or setting up income assistance for struggling farmers.

It has been revealed that the World Food Programme first tested its forecast-based financing program in Zimbabwe during the 2015 El Niño: Delivering cash to families in one district facing drought helped them to sustain their quantity and quality of food, while a neighboring district that didn’t receive cash aid saw a massive drop. This year, the WFP has been delivering cash and other assistance, including, for example, more than 3,000 airtight silos for farmers in Guatemala to help them safely store grain. As of October, the program claims it has reached 28 million people across 15 countries with early warning information and assistance.

Cash is strapped for such programs, though. Funds for global aid were down 30 percent in 2025 from their 2022 peak and are still falling, making it hard for the WFP and others to do their work. In Somalia, the WFP helped 10 million people during a drought in 2022; today, in the face of similar conditions, says Choularton, they can afford to reach fewer than a million.

In a recent development, advanced warning is good, claims Lobell, but challenges will still abound, and even harder times may lie ahead as El Niños pile on top of climate change. The peaks of strong El Niños are almost always followed by record-breaking years for the global average temperature. The anomalously hot years of 1998, 2016, and 2024 (the current record holder) all followed hot on the heels of El Niño peaks the year before. While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says Hausfather.

Global warming, of course, also has impacts on food supply. Last year, Lobell published a paper showing that total wheat, barley, maize, rice, and soybean yields are now altogether about 5 percent lower overall than they would have been in a world without climate change. “To a lot of people, that sounds like a small number. But the kind of shocks that we talk about can be far smaller than that,” he indicates. “It doesn’t take much of a supply shift to have an vital effect on people’s lives.”.

Because the specific places that get warmer and drier during El Niños are different from the specific places that get warmer and drier from climate change, researchers caution that what we see in 2026 won’t be a precise forerunner of things to come. But how we deal with this temporary challenge does say something about the resilience of our food systems, says Lobell, and it will reveal how we might cope in the future with other climate disruptions to crops. “That’s one of the significant questions,” he says. “How much can you adapt when the conditions are bad?”.

#2793. Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1706 w)

Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
  • For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt.
  • They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.

They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.

According to recent reports, fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.

Now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine mentioned.

It has been revealed that the experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” said Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”.

When he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined swiftly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.

When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.

Convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.

It has been revealed that they considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.

Through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining demonstrated no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.

By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.

For six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.

When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples showed higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.

In a recent development, during metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.

He devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.

It was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.

According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.

According to recent reports, for Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he said. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.

The idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.

“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran remarked.

Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, said Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.

“This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he noted of the latest work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.

Another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, said Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.

In a recent development, ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he said. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.

However, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet stated. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.

For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.

“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet said, “right there under our feet.”.

#2790. Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (938 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday.
  • It has been revealed that AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026.
  • Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

It has been revealed that AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power people latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a latest couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

Recent findings suggest that some customers value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

Industry observers note that it’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently unveiled that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get consumers in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

According to recent reports, banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.

Sources indicate that “The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”.

It has been revealed that even though outliers exist, many consumers are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” states Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, substantial-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

It has been revealed that cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Industry observers note that certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express revealed that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” People have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even debuted an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.

Sources indicate that whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.
